issues.item: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: Compulsive exercise is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other selected items cluster around hypervigilance, dissociation, memory disorganisation, and danger-based appraisals after terrorism. Excessive exercise does not clearly serve or connect to those symptoms, making it look like a strategy for a different presentation unless additional context were present.

issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is disproportionately severe relative to the rest of the selected profile and is not well supported by the surrounding appraisals. The other appraisals focus on danger and bodily unreliability, while the threat/memory items emphasize hyperarousal and fragmented recall. This suicidal-hopelessness appraisal can occur in PTSD, but here it stands out as insufficiently linked to the rest of the formulation and item set.

vignette: Elena was nineteen when the coordinated attacks shattered the morning market in her hometown. She remembered the initial roar of the first explosion, then a sequence of concussive blasts that turned concrete into shrapnel. Amid the chaos, a man lunged toward her with a weapon, his movements so sudden and violent that her nervous system locked into immediate survival mode. She escaped by bolting into a narrow alley, but the incident left a permanent shift in how she navigated the world. In the months that followed, she could not find words to describe what happened, and distinct fragments of the day simply vanished from her mind. Yet, when those gaps closed and the memory of the violence returned, it did not bring grief; it brought a searing rage that made her jaw clench and her palms sweat. Because she could not reconstruct a coherent timeline of the bombing, she felt no sense of safety in her own judgment, which only deepened her conviction that the world remained a dangerously unpredictable place. Her conviction that the world was a dangerous place, paired with her belief that she had to be on guard all the time, quickly dictated her daily behavior. She began avoiding eye contact with coworkers and strangers alike, convinced that sustained gazes would invite unwanted attention or escalation. When the anxiety grew too heavy to process, she deliberately tried to leave her body or blank out, detaching herself from the present moment as a way to survive the overwhelm. This internal shift toward avoidance directly stemmed from her negative appraisals, which framed her only viable path as withdrawal and self-erasure. This same belief structure fundamentally altered her threat processing. Because she had come to accept the world as a dangerous place and her own vigilance as a necessity, her perception of danger became hyper-attuned to the environment. Sudden movements by others instantly put her on guard, transforming ordinary shifts in the warehouse aisles into perceived emergencies. Her nervous system learned to read the distribution center's metal shelving and falling cartons as potential weapon fire, ensuring that threat was never far from her awareness. The fragmented nature of her recall further dictated her coping strategies. Whenever the memory gaps widened or the rage on recall threatened to surface, Elena felt compelled to check her surroundings repeatedly, pacing the perimeter of her workspace to regain a sense of control. The inability to process the event linguistically left her stranded in a state of physiological readiness, which naturally drove her to dissociate deliberately whenever the warehouse hum grew too loud. Her memory symptoms consistently channeled her into these rigid, controlling behaviors. Her relationship with the past directly fueled her present danger sense. As the memory gaps persisted and the rage upon recall flared without resolution, her baseline alertness sharpened accordingly. She found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, lying awake with her heart hammering, certain that the violence she had survived would return if she let her guard down. The unprocessed trauma continuously fed her threat system, making stillness feel like surrender. The heightened threat perception quickly hardened into rigid coping habits. When the startle response made her jump at the clang of falling pallets, or when night vigilance stripped her of rest, Elena retreated into avoidance. The constant scanning of the environment, once a temporary measure, became an automatic reflex she deployed whenever her nervous system threatened to overload. Her threat symptoms actively dictated her maladaptive strategies, locking her into a pattern of defensive withdrawal. This state of chronic alarm actively interfered with her cognitive processing. The relentless threat in movements and the startle response kept her amygdala in overdrive, which systematically eroded her ability to encode or retrieve memories. As she remained locked in a cycle of scanning and bracing, the memory gaps widened further, leaving her unable to find words to make sense of her own reactions. Her threat monitoring directly sabotaged her capacity for recall. Over time, the strategies she adopted to cope began to rewrite her internal narrative. Every time she avoided eye contact or forced herself to dissociate, she interpreted her body's retreat as proof that she could no longer trust her own body. The avoidance, meant to protect her, instead confirmed her negative appraisals, convincing her that the world was dangerous and that she was fundamentally unsafe in it. Her maladaptive strategies actively reinforced her negative appraisals. These same behaviors kept her nervous system trapped in a state of false alarm. By constantly checking her surroundings instead of allowing her physiology to downshift, Elena ensured that her threat detection system never received the signal to rest. This self-perpetuating loop meant that sudden movements by others continued to trigger immediate guards, and her startle response remained permanently dialed to maximum sensitivity. Her avoidance tactics actively sustained her threat symptoms. Now twenty-four and single, Elena sits on a worn couch in the clinic waiting room, her posture rigid and her gaze fixed on the floor. The warehouse job, once a simple means of income, has become a minefield of near-miss episodes and supervisor reprimands for her inability to collaborate or respond normally to shift changes. She finally sought help because the dissociative episodes began spilling into her commute, and she grew terrified of driving through intersections. What she hopes for is quiet, while what she fears most is that trying to heal will only make the danger feel closer than it already does.
